summary:
Guinea's 2016 Penal Code, Article 274, punishes consensual same-sex conduct with six months to three years' imprisonment, a fine of GNF 500,000 to 1,000,000, or both. The provision replaced Article 325 of the 1998 Penal Code, which criminalised the same conduct through indecency provisions and set a lower minimum fine. Where the conduct involves violence or attempted violence, the sentence rises to five to ten years, and acts with a person under 21 carry the maximum penalty.

Enforcement reaches people who are not charged with conduct. Police arrest on the basis of clothing and appearance, and Article 274 functions as a standing basis for extortion, with release commonly secured by payment to officers. A 2024 Universal Periodic Review stakeholder submission reports LGBTQ people held for up to five days despite the 48-hour legal limit, most released only after paying bribes or fines.

Transgender women are arrested and imprisoned on the stated pretext of protecting them from community violence, then held in male prisons where they often experience sexual violence. LGBTQ people in custody are frequently abused.

In 2023 the Office for the Protection of Women, Children, and Morals added a unit to investigate same-sex conduct. Security forces have arrested, harassed and used violence against LGBTQ people accused of disrupting social order. In 2016 and 2017 the organization Afrique Arc-en-Ciel Conakry reported gay men jailed and fined for release.

Guinea provides no legal gender recognition and no recognition of same-sex unions. No laws protect LGBTQ people from discrimination in health services, and LGBTQ people face discrimination when seeking healthcare, housing, education and employment.

Law L/2024/001/CNT/SGG of January 12, 2024 on HIV Prevention, Care, and Protection defines members of sexual minorities to include gays, lesbians, bisexuals, intersex and transgender people whether or not they self-identify. Ordinance No. 056/2009/PRG/SGG on HIV/AIDS lists sexual minorities as a vulnerable and marginalized group.

A 2024 UPR stakeholder report describes a hostile, sometimes lethal environment for LGBTQ people, with threats of physical violence and discrimination on orientation, gender-identity and expression grounds, and widespread stigmatisation that hinders reporting of violence. A survey spanning 2021 to 2023 found 87 percent of Guineans would dislike or strongly dislike having a gay neighbor.

The 2023 U.S. State Department Human Rights Report found that LGBTQ groups exist but cannot obtain legal recognition despite no law barring it, that most LGBTQ Guineans do not disclose publicly, and that LGBTQ people are cast as part of a Western imperialist agenda attributed to the United States and France. Some LGBTQ Guineans have been internally displaced to escape areas whose religious and cultural norms endanger them.

Families arrange forced heterosexual marriages, and religious, cultural and familial pressure is used to attempt to convert LGBTQ people, a pressure that falls heavily on younger people.

Section 9.9.30(b) of the Guinea Aeronautical Regulations (2022), issued by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, bars competent government agencies from using Passenger Name Record data that reveals an individual's sex life or sexual orientation, alongside racial, ethnic, political, religious, trade-union or health data. The text gives no further detail on entry screening, visa rules, or border checks for trans or LGBTQ travelers.
tangentialFactors:
The 2011 U.S. State Department report described homosexuality as socially, religiously and culturally taboo with no LGBTQ organizations in the country; the 2023 report found that LGBTQ groups do now exist but lack legal recognition. The 2011 report also documented security-force torture, prison abuse and FGM in Guinea, indicating a broader pattern of abuse in detention.

In 2010 Prime Minister Lansana Kouyate stated that consensual same-sex activity was wrong and should be illegal and that sexual orientation should not be a human right, an official statement of hostility on record.

Adoption is open to a couple married at least five years or an unmarried person aged at least 30 with a 15-year age gap, and Guinean law does not specifically bar LGBTQ persons from adopting.

There is no legal gender recognition process in Guinea and no recognition of same-sex unions, so trans residents cannot obtain documents matching their gender identity and cannot marry a partner of the same gender.

outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not document any trans-specific killing or violence rate for Guinea against which a general homicide baseline could be compared, so no trans-specific violence magnitude can be stated. The 2024 UPR stakeholder report's description of a 'sometimes lethal' environment is qualitative and undated as to specific incidents.

The most recent specific documented incidents of arrest and jailing in this record are from 2016 and 2017 (Afrique Arc-en-Ciel Conakry reports) and the 2023 addition of an investigative unit; no later individual case is documented.

Section 9.9.30(b) of the 2022 Aeronautical Regulations restricts use of Passenger Name Record data revealing sexual orientation, but the text gives no detail on entry screening, visa rules, or border checks for trans travelers; whether any trans-specific document or screening practice exists at entry is not sourced.

The 87 percent survey figure covers attitudes toward a gay neighbor, is not trans-specific, and spans 2021 to 2023; no equivalent figure for attitudes toward transgender people is available in the inventory.
